Even urbanized areas with well-established regional transit based on fixed-route, fixed-schedule bus or rail technology are beginning to integrate ODT to service lower-density suburbs where fixed-route service is inefficient and provide community circulation services in high-density regions and connection to larger-vehicle regional transit services. In this context, the service model is no longer fixed routes or schedules; mobility is provided by individually dispatched small- to medium-sized vehicles operating on a range of demand scenarios from real- time on-demand (similar to most ride-hailing commercial services) to a ride request placed in advance for a future trip, perhaps 30–90 minutes in advance. In some ways, modern ODT services can be described as having evolved from paratransit and taxi service to use modern computing and communications for higher service levels and flexibility. Fixed-route, fixed- schedule AV service may still be used within a district, even with larger-sized vehicles, but this service would be limited to interconnecting high-demand activity centers within the district such as shopping plazas and mobility hubs servicing regional transit services—with most of the dispersed demand within the district serviced by ODT. Figure 2 illustrates the premise of a variety of services, with varying vehicle sizes and types servicing a district. AV transit services are deployed to supply various forms of on-demand dispatched services as well as conventional transit services along fixed routes. ODT services both real-time trip requests, comparable to commercial ride-hailing, as well as scheduled trip requests. NLR’s investigations of Houston METRO’s curb2curb service has been particularly insightful regarding the latter (Armbrister, Young, Lott, Powell, Henao and Andrade 2025). This on-demand service typically has passengers making reservations between 30 minutes and 2 hours in advance of a requested pickup time, primarily through a mobile phone app, though reservations through telephone service are also available. ODT is similar to commercial ride-hailing services but with the likelihood of any trip to be conducted as ride-sharing or ride-pooling as a core component within the system design. Illustrated in Figure 2 are AV ride-hailing services, colloquially referred to as “robotaxis.” Although most commercial ride-hailing services such as Uber and Lyft are dominated by real- time private trip requests, they also provide prescheduled rides (e.g., reservation made 30 minutes or more in advance), most notably for airport trips, while still supplying direct origin-to- destination service. Multiple forms of AV transit are shown to emphasize that an AMD will likely comprise multiple fleets of AVs, each providing distinct types of services—which together provide complete community circulation and connection to regional transit service. Not shown in Figure 2 but a vital part of any AMD are pedestrians, bicycles, and other forms of private or shared micromobility that provide nonmotorized mobility and active transportation within the district in accordance with the needs of users.
